utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. First, I undertook last week to report to the Chamber the Prosecution's position with respect to the recent Appeals Chamber decision regarding adjudicated facts. Later on today, the Prosecution will file an application, so I won't go into too much detail now, other than to note that the Prosecution will be seeking judiciary notice of a number of facts reformulated to be consistent with the Appeals Chamber's decision as well as to address some of the concerns raised by this Trial Chamber in its original decision on some of those facts. We will also be re-calling investigator Barry Hogan. That will be the only witness that we would recall and we will recall him to deal with some of the rejected or removed adjudicated facts that deal with the location of the confrontation line. We expect this testimony to be quite brief on -- on this. Your Honour, I have one other matter. I would ask to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The witness may be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time by addressing the Prosecution on the following matter: There has been some discussion about a transcription error in Witness Celanovic's prior testimony which was admitted as P1451. I refer to transcript page 11248. In the meantime, the Popovic transcript has been corrected by CLSS and this was filed in the Popovic case on the 6th of November, 2013. The Prosecution is hereby instructed to upload a new version of P1451, in line with CLSS's revision, within one week, and the Registry is already instructed to make the necessary replacement once uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Mr. Brown, before we resume, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the some declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi will now continue his examination. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P431, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In your report, you talk about the strategic objectives Mr. Karadzic lays out at this session. Based on your review of documents, were similar objectives being pursued before the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I believe the strategic objectives as a whole are about identifying territory that the Bosnian Serbs deemed as theirs, and I don't know -- I think in my report, I don't argue that the strategic goals were, in essence, a start point. Territory had already been taken control of in some areas prior to this assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what do you see as the importance of the discussion of the objectives at this session?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when I was writing my report at the time, there were some comments in some of the military documents that I was seeing, which were talking about goals and objectives of the Serbian people. And what I wanted to try and do was find out further what those were, because I felt that it was usual that militaries work to some degree or some form of political guidance, unless it's a military dictatorship, I guess, so that was the background to my interest in this, and this is why I looked at the assembly session. And it seemed to me that at the very time the VRS was being established formally at this assembly session that clearly articulated political goals were being disseminated by the political leadership to the military ensuring that everybody, including the civilians who were present but also the new commander of the VRS and other military figures who were present there, were aware of the political objectives of the Bosnian Serbs, and I believe that strategic goals crystallised those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You described General Mladic as having sounded a cautionary note about the objectives at this session, and that's beginning at paragraph 1.45 of your Krajina report. Can you describe for the Chamber why you see his remarks that way?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when, in particular, in relation to strategic goal number 1, to the issue of separation, when Karadzic makes mention of that and also the delegates themselves make mention and some of them talk very specifically about resettlement or the moving of people, or the moving of non-Serbs has already happened, for example, in Krupe, it seemed that some of his comments seemed to articulate that this policy of moving peoples around was a dangerous one. And he himself talks about people are not pawns to move around. People sive -- you can't sive people, where some will stay and others will leave, and he uses the phrase genocide, and that the political leadership will have to explain this if it becomes known. And it seems to stand out as being something of a warning or a cautionary note that this is what is the reality of what is going to happen and also what is already happened in some municipalities prior to this assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, what we have in front of us on our screen that seems that the English version and the B/C/S version do not match, at least not the first page. Because in the English, although it seems to be also related to the 16th Session held on the 12th of May, it starts in a totally different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll check that over the break. I think it's possible that one is the minutes and one is the transcript. But we'll -- we'll check. Perhaps even before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the case from what I understand. Let's proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 34 in the English; I believe page 33 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're in part of General Mladic's speech here, and the transcript records him saying: "Let us not only put our minds into what we are doing. But let us also" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It will be in the middle of the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Give us time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. In the English on the right, Your Honour, there's a sentence -- there's line that starts: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Serbian Republic of Krajina." I'm reading two lines below that. It's about maybe a quarter of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: General Mladic says: "Let us not only put our minds into what we are doing. But let us also speak" -- sorry, "think thoroughly about it and let us be cautious about when to keep mum. No, the thing that we are doing needs to be guarded as our deepest secret." You refer to this language in paragraph 1.48 of your Krajina report. What importance do you ascribe to this language?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think General Mladic here is bearing in mind his previous comment. He -- he -- to make it publicly known that this issue of separation, in particular, or marking out the boundaries, would be, if it was publicly known, very difficult for the Bosnian Serbs. And here what he is saying is, We must keep this to ourselves, we must make our goals appealing externally, but people need to read between the lines about what it really means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the same session -- if we could go to page 47 of the English and 43 of the B/C/S. We are towards the top of the page in a speech by Mr. Krajisnik, and he says, beginning in the first line on the English: "We are at war, and it will be possible to solve this thing with the Muslims and Croats only by war. And the politics will be instrumental in bringing it to an end." He continues about three lines, four lines later: "Please, if we acquire the territories which we agree on and have conceived of today, plus the corridor we get up there, we will have done, this generation will have done so much for the Serbian people that this debt will be impossible to repay. What will happen in reality, we... leave that to time, but it will be easier to achieve this now, once we establish the Serbian army which could have been done earlier." Do you relate this comment to the relationship between the VRS and the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. I think by this time it's clear that they view -- the establishment of the army is going to be used in order to fulfil the goals stated, and that, indeed, is what I would argue happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 02677, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a document from the 1st Partizan Brigade dated 14 May 1992. Were those strategic objectives also communicated to VRS officers who were not in attendance at the 16th Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is a document that would identify that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And let's look at some of the key features of this document now. Starting on page 1 in both languages this refers in part to the transformation of the JNA - we see that at point 2 - and messages from the meeting of the armed forces of Serbian Krajina and the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Banja Luka on 12 May 1992 at point 3. Do you relate to that the assembly session that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. This -- this is the agenda, and -- and it clearly identifies the session two days before this. This is a meeting in a subordinate formation of the corps. The 30th Division was a subordinate unit of the 1st Krajina Corps. And it's commander was Stanislav Galic, who subsequently became the corps commander in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps a bit later that year. So here the -- that officer, Colonel Branko Basara, who was a brigade commander who we talked about yesterday from the 6th Brigade, and others are meeting with municipal leaders in the zone of the division discussing the issues that come from the assembly session a few days before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2, it reflects Colonel Galic briefing the group about security conditions in various municipalities. And then on page 3 in the English and the B/C/S, in the third paragraph at the top, refers to the president of the Mrkonjic Grad Srpska Opstina presenting the conclusions from the meeting held in Banja Luka which it describes as strategic goals formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka. Do you have any comment on the substance of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here they're discussing the very issues that were referenced at the assembly session. There was some discussion in that session about the army not taking so much territory. It can defend it, that's referenced here, and then they articulate the six goals that were discussed by or presented by Radovan Karadzic. So, in essence, I think this is dissemination the very same message that was -- that was articulated at assembly session down military chain and also to local municipal bodies. There are a couple of other issues of this document that have some interest. The previous page, for example, in relation to Kljuc, it is also talking about military units that are deploying there. So already at this stage you have units of the corps conducting operations to secure that territory, for example. But, in essence, I think the importance of the document is that the message of the 16th Assembly Session is being disseminated down at low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 02677 as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02677 receives number P2867, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2867 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we next have P2412, marked for identification. It's a Sanski Most Crisis Staff document dated the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, you describe some of the first VRS operations in late May 1992 in the ARK and I want to go through the lead-up to those operations briefly. As this comes up, can you describe for the Chamber the patterns you saw in how those operations were conducted?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's -- there's quite a lot of detail, and some of that, I hope, is contained in the report. But in summary, I think there were a number of similar patterns in a number of those municipalities, including Sanski Most. Often included decisions or declarations by the local Crisis Staff, the ARK Crisis Staff, to initiate operations by the police to surrender illegally held weapons. Deadlines for those surrender. Meetings of Crisis Staffs, which included military, police, and political representatives. Establishing plans to conduct operations in those municipalities. Deployments of units, military units and TO units and attacks on predominantly -- or exclusively, as I saw from the document, non-Serb villages, which would then result in large numbers of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to take you through three documents now and then ask you some questions after we've seen all three. In this first document, it reflects at point 4 on page 1 in both languages that Nedjeljko Rasula and Nedo Anicic are directed to contact the president of the assembly of the autonomous region concerning the question of disarming paramilitary formations. Lower down on point 9, now on page 3 in the B/C/S, it opines that the question of disarming paramilitary formations has to be approached comprehensively and says to co-ordinate with the Prijedor and Kljuc municipalities. So that's the first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 06914. This is a document from the ARK Crisis Staff issued 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Under point 1, this document directs: "The State Security Service of the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall consistently carry out the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the disarming of paramilitary units and individuals who are illegally in possession of weapons and ammunition."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we turn now to 65 ter 16919 [Realtime transcript read in error "16916"], please. This is an instruction from CSB Banja Luka issued the same day. As it comes up, I note perhaps my speed was off again, but I was recorded to say "16916" and intended "16919." And could we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This document is communicated to several different chiefs and to the Ministry of the Interior for information. And it provides several directions for public security stations which must undertake, in part, making concrete plans that include operational findings about illegally owned weapons, the time and place of measures to be taken against groups and individuals. And it says, just below that, the second point from the bottom: "This actively can only be implemented by authorised officials and the military police of the Banja Luka Corps." Do you see these three documents as related?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were -- they were part of a chain of documents, in fact, which I think is explained further in my report, emanating initially from the ARK initially requesting the police to start this planning process and that involved later an engagement of the military in those activities and plans too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When the documents discuss disarming paramilitaries, who do they mean?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents themselves at face value don't make any differentiation about who they are meaning. But, in reality, as events panned out on the ground, the operations that were conducted on the back of these decisions from the municipalities I saw were against non-Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender those three documents, one at a time. First, P2412, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- I do remember that it was part of a series and which was MFI'd, to say the least, I think it was on the 25th of September. But the exact reasons, I don't remember why it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's an associated exhibit pending a decision of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, no objections. Madam Registrar. Yes, we have the number already. So, therefore, P2412 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, 65 ter 06914.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06914 receives number P2868, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2868 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And third, Your Honour, 65 ter 16919.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16919 receives number P2869, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2869 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask that we have 65 ter 07992. This is a 5th Corps document issued the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What we see here, sir, is described just below the heading to the commander of the Prijedor region as a request for information on the disposition of units from the 5th Corps to the Prijedor region. What importance do you ascribe to this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document has been sent by General Talic to Colonel Vladimir Arsic, who was the commander of the Prijedor region as well as the commander of the 43 Motorised Brigade, and he is requesting information from him about his own troop strength and locations of the brigades and units in that zone but also requesting the disposition of paramilitaries or the estimation of paramilitaries and paramilitary strength in his zone. And he identifies the zone in paragraph 1. The zone is, in essence, a circle. If you put Prijedor in the centre, it's a curricular area between -- halfway between Banja Luka and Prijedor and up to Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you see it as connected with the disarmament orders we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is General Talic trying to prepare the brigade and to get a -- an idea from his subordinate in preparation for operations that were conducted there a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 07125, please. While it comes up, I'd tender 65 ter 07992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07992 receives number P2870, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document, when it comes up, will be the minutes of the Prijedor Council for National Defence dated 15 May. And we see at the top of the first page a list of attendees, including Colonel Arsic as well as Pero Colic and Radmilo Zeljaja. Are those also military officers?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, sir. Pero Colic was the commander of the 5th Kozara Brigade, and Zeljaja was Colonel Arsic's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 2. At the bottom of this page, it says: "The public security station in concert with the army command should draft the plan of disarmament ..." Do you relate this to the previous documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they're all connected and the Crisis Staff was the form in which the various organisations could co-ordinate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At point 3, this reflects the Prijedor Crisis Staff's decision to: "Start the transformation of both TO Staffs and form a unified command for control and command of all the units formed in the territory of the municipality." Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the -- the issues - I actually think it was referenced at the 16th Assembly Session - was that the Territorial Defence should be -- should be integrated into the new VRS and the TO should come under the command of the VRS. And I believe that this is probably a reflection of that. The TO Staffs did in the 1st Krajina Corps zone -- they were -- they were integrated into the corps and generally became light infantry brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 07125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As -- as I could see briefly, I think we saw the misrepresentation of this document. It's not Crisis Staff document. It's some other body from Prijedor. So all this testimony is wrong. It's dealt as a document from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think I've described it myself in -- in -- consistent with what was on page 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But just, Mr. Brown, in a -- related to your conclusion that the Crisis Staff was involved in this document, we see on the list of attendees Milomir Stakic. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Crisis Staff, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I renew my question to tendered the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness can say was Mr. Stakic member of any other body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't, Your Honour. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, whatever the description of the document is, it remains that -- let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- minutes of the fourth meeting of the Council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. That is how it is described. And I think that's the -- and then it says who attended. And the agenda contained at least elements which refer to the Crisis Staff; for example, agenda item 1: Decision on the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff. Mr. Lukic, have the -- has the identity of the document been sufficiently clarified to lift your objection or?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know at this moment Crisis Staff did not exist at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- so whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I saw this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question is, some questions were put, which were rather about the substance than about the quality of the -- what the meeting was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously the witness does not have any understanding about this body and the role of Mr. Stakic in this body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness described that -- what this document directs was, in fact, carried out and its relationship to other pieces of evidence that have been admitted. I'd submit that that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put a question to you, Mr. Brown. What is your understanding of this body, Council for National Defence of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly? What was the function of this body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's been some time, sir, since I looked in detail at the activities within Prijedor municipality in detail. I did compile a report early on whilst I was at the ICTY on this. I could refer to that maybe in the break and have a look. But I would surmise that this is a Defence Council -- local municipal Defence Council body that brings together security personnel and key civilian personnel on issues relating to security and defence matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You see here, on the top of the page, that Mr. Stakic is referred to as president of the council who chaired the meeting. Earlier you said that Mr. Stakic was head of the Crisis Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am -- I believe he was head of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor, sir. He may have been concurrently the head, and, it would seem from this document, that he was concurrently president of this National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic suggested that this moment, 15th of May, 1992, the Crisis Staff was not set up yet. What is your understanding about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I would have to go back to my Prijedor report, but I believe the Crisis Staff was functioning by this time. But if Mr. Lukic has other documents that could demonstrate that that wasn't the case, I'd be happy to look at them. But it's on my understanding that the Crisis Staff was established then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you look at the agenda, item 1 is decision on the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff. How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Clearly have been some discussion about -- about the establishment of this Crisis Staff. Whether it was established on this day, I don't know. But it isn't an area that I have done a lot of work in recently, so I'd have to reserve judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The document will be admitted under -- into evidence. The number would be, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 07125 receives number P2871, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2871 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I've checked the transcript, and I should apologise. It appears at page 17, line 5, I misspoke and used the term Crisis Staff incorrectly. And that may have led to the confusion. And I -- my error, I think has been clarified by the Chamber, but I thought I should apologise on record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The document at least mentions the organisation and functioning of the Crisis Staff and decisions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The draft was adopted for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I'm now going to turn to the creation of the VRS a few days later and the mobilisation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 03688, the document dated 20 May 1992 and signed by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us the importance of this document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mobilisation -- even though the VRS was formally established on the 12th, there had been a lot of discussion at the 16th Assembly Session that there needed to be mobilisation into the army. It notes in the first paragraph that the Presidency had issued a mobilisation and the timing of this is probably of interest, because the 19th, 20th, was when the JNA were formally meant to withdraw from Bosnia. So even though there had been discussions on the 12th of May about mobilising and the formation of the army, it most likely would seem that they delayed this instruction because they didn't want to look like they were somehow disrupting this technical withdrawal of the JNA on the 19th, 20th. So this is probably why it came out on this day, in essence, immediately after the JNA was technically meant to withdraw from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 03688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03688 receives number P2872, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 28410, please. This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps dated 21 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And here at the beginning, it refers to the decision of the Presidency initiating a general mobilisation. What importance do you ascribe to that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Talic's instructions to his corps about mobilisation and it's reacting to the Presidency decision, so he is clearly responding to that tasking chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have page 2 of the English, please, still page 1 of the B/C/S. In document at point 1, directs subordinate units to: "Immediately establish direct contact with municipal and military and territorial organs on the ground offering expert and materiel support for the mobilisation process." I'd refer Your Honours to point 8 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this the point that you were referring to yesterday, or one of them, where General Talic emphasises co-operation with the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he references this in a couple of locations in this particular document. Co-operation was already occurring, and I think what he is doing here is re-emphasising the importance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to point 6, still on page 2 in the English and also in the B/C/S now, it says: "Explain to conscripts as they arrive the goals of our struggle and brief them on their duties and rights. Do not enlist waverers or suspicious persons in the units." What do you take from this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think here he's emphasising that individuals who come into his corps have to have the goals explained to them in order for them to understand why they will be fighting. And I would link this to the goals that were articulated in the assembly session a few days prior to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if -- if -- is it visible from this document what the gentleman just said that he connects it with the goals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different matter. The testimony of the witness should be clearly distinguished from the document which is before us, because wrong testimony is not, as far as I am aware of, is not a reason for non-admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't object to the document. Only I wanted maybe clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In cross-examination you -- of course you can ask the witness how he possibly could have deduced from this document what you consider to be a wrong conclusion. That's no problem. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28410 receives number P2873, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2873 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 05978. It's another 1st Krajina Corps document issued the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On page 1 of the English and B/C/S, this document reports that, "A major transformation of the army has taken place," refers to the formation of an army of the Serbian Republic of BH towards the top of page 1. Turning to page 2 of the English, I want to ask you about two points on this page. First, the document reads at the top: "The constituent Serbian people who live on around 65 per cent of the area and represent more than 35 per cent of the population of BH must struggle for complete separation from the Muslim and Croatian peoples and" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, whenever you are reading your speed of speech goes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll try and be more careful about that, Your Honour, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And another advice: You should always indicate where this can be found in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In -- this is in point 2, so it's toward -- at the very bottom of the first page you can see the 65 per cent [B/C/S spoken] 35 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My pronunciation is quite terrible but hopefully that is sufficient to direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the last five lines we find the reference to 35 and 65 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, having located the language, what importance do you ascribe to it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that's written by General Talic's commander -- assistant commander for morale and legal affairs, Colonel Vukelic, Milutin Vukelic, and it's a summary document from him to be send down to the units identifying the situation as they are, and it clearly identifies that it would seem to echo the issue of separation -- separation from communities and forming their own state which of course was the core of Karadzic's goals in -- although Karadzic doesn't mention the percentages, the separation of communities and forming their own state and if would seem to echo those -- those objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, below point 3 on page 2 of the B/C/S, the document reads: "The Main Staff has been appointed and Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, who has commanded large formations on the Knin front very successfully since the start of this war, has been appointed commander. "All other major elements of unified organisation and command and control have been set up." Is all of that consistent with the expert conclusions you're able to draw based on your review of VRS documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic had been appointed and the Main Staff was functioning, and, at this time corps reports were going up to the Main Staff which seemed to agree with the statement here that the -- that the army was -- was up and running.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in your report, do you also refer to direction as early as this time coming down from the Main Staff to the corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note it's time for the break. I'd tendered this document as a public.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could, I would just like to add at the very end of this document Colonel Vukelic states that the contents of this document should be thrashed out or disseminated to soldiers. So it isn't just an internal document for the staff, that it is meant to be disseminated down to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05978 receives number P2874, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I put on the record. The Chamber puts on the public record that in its decision filed confidential on the 14th of November, 2013, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's 33rd Rule 92 bis motion and admitted the evidence of Witness RM275 pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We take a break. We'll come back at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As he's coming in, I should apologise for a lack of precision in my estimate. I think it may be an additional 12- to 1800 seconds beyond what I had initially estimated. I apologise to the Chamber for the, again, lack of precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. And compared to what? To your initial assessment or to your later assessments? I mean, in minutes what would it be and how much still would you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the -- the most practical way to say it, Your Honour, is that it will be this session and perhaps the beginning, 15 minutes or so, of the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated. Please be seated, Mr. Brown. You may proceed. The clock is ticking, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm very conscious of that, Mr. President. Could we, please, have Exhibit P247.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to turn now, Mr. Brown, to a very brief discussion of how these disarmament operations were carried out. This is a 1st Krajina Corps report from 27 May 1992, and we see it's titled: "Report on elimination of Green Berets in wider area of Kozarac village." And it notes at point 1 the dates of the conflict. Notes the total strength of the Green Berets at point 3. It was 1500 to 2.000 men without heavy weapons. And then notes the results on point 4. Do you have any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would just seem to be a summary of what had happened, in particular, in the brigade 43rd, 343rd brigade that they had been very quickly successful in their operations in that area. It follows on in a way from the disarmament plans, but it identifies that they were successful and they had relatively few casualties and that a large number of people were now prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned both the military and the police in describing who was to carry out those operations. I have two questions about that. First, on the basis of the documents you reviewed, could you conclude what role the military had in the operations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military had the primary role in terms of the combat operations in these areas. You should also note in this document that the Prijedor Brigade is using heavy weapons, Howitzer, artillery, and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Chamber has received a great deal of evidence about these operations, so for now I will just move to asking you if you could characterise the reporting from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff about the conduct of these operations.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they sent daily combat reports, as I discussed yesterday. Usually these would report that the territory -- operations that were ongoing, they would invariably report that the territory was being secured. Often these operations lasted a relatively short space of time but they were reported up to the Main Staff in daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now two documents related to the end of these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 02840.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is another 1st Krajina Corps document from a few days later sent to the Main Staff. And, in this document, right above point 2 in both languages I would just point you to the description that says: "Muslim and Croatian families are stopping at nothing to find ways of moving out of the areas affected by the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 02838, please. I think we have it in the B/C/S but not yet in the English. In the third paragraph of page 1 in both languages, the 1st Krajina Corps notes: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the region of Bosnian Krajina" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "... has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out. Those departing will not be allowed to return." Do you have any comment on these two documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that the 1st Krajina Corps know that large numbers of Muslims and Croats are -- are leaving. It, to me, cuts to this issue of separation. This document was also written by Milutin Vukelic as well from the corps. And it would seem that the issue of separation and the movement out of populations is -- is -- is -- is being undertaken in those areas at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And based on the previous documents we've reviewed today, and other documents you've reviewed, two of the other consequences for the local population that we've seen on the screen are killings and captures. In your view, was the Main Staff also being informed and the 1st Krajina Corps also aware of those consequences?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There -- there are references in relation to killings. There are some references in my report to specific 1st Krajina Corps documents that note killings and I cite those. There are -- are a number of references that large numbers of individuals are being placed in detention camps and that is also being reported in -- in their daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tendered these last two documents. 02838 first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number P2875, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2875 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And P -- and, sorry, 02840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02840 receives number P2876, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2876 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could we have Exhibit P353, page 38 in the English and 37 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As this comes up, sir, you've just testified that, at this time, the Main Staff had received reports of the expulsions from the ARK, the prisoners taken by the 1st Krajina Corps, and the capture of very large numbers of non-Serbs. What was the next primary VRS operation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They secured territory around this late May/early June period and the big key operation they were involved in, in the middle of June was Operation Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to explore the genesis of that operation to some degree now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have, please, page 38 in the English. And here we see the beginning of a meeting with the leadership of the Serbian republic. Could we turn to the bottom of page 41 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, may I take it that on the previous pages we would find the date on which this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- yes, Your Honour, I apologise. And I believe it's 31 May, but it's on the previous pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And pages 39 and 40 are a continuation of the same meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr. Lukic, that if there's any disagreement there, that you would point at it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, sir, in both languages, General Mladic records: "If there is response to mobilisation into the 1st Krajina Corps then we clear the Posavina of Croats." If we turn to the next page in both languages, please. Just above the middle of the page and just above, Your Honour, you can see the date there, 1 June 1992. So this is the conclusion of the meeting on the previous day. General Mladic writes: "We must have corridor in the Posavina; part of Sarajevo; operations group at the Drina." Now to which strategic objectives do those relate?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategic objective 2 was the corridor in the Posavina, and strategic objective 5 was to divide or separate parts of Sarajevo. So it refers directly to these.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have P474, page 2 in English and B/C/S. This is going to be directive 1 coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'll ask, as it does, do you relate these notes to what you saw in directive 1?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do. There was a sequence of events, I think, emanating from this meeting on the 31st. There's also a comment in that meeting as, Are the corps commanders coming to the meeting on Wednesday. Wednesday being the 3rd of June. The day after this meeting on the 31st, the VRS send out instruction to all corps commanders to come to a meeting on the 3rd of June, in which they're to bring a map with their corps areas and discuss issues relating to their corps. That document is cited in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours just for the record, I believe Mr. Brown's describing Exhibit D00098. So let's turn to page 2 of the English. And if we could still have the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S, I apologise. First, the goals are described: "(a) secure parts of Sarajevo with a majority Serbian population to 'ocistiti,' the wider area of Sarajevo airport and 'ocistiti,' its wider area of remaining groups and of individuals belonging to the enemy." Under point(b), now on page 2 in the B/C/S, this document directs that the VRS: "Ensure contact between Semberija and Bosnian Krajina." Do you relate these to the notebook entries we just reviewed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I very much do. I think there was the meeting on the 31st, meeting of the corps commanders. Concurrently with this meeting there was a meeting of the senior leadership on the same day, and it's clear that what fell from those discussions and meetings was this operative directive, and the contents of this directive are predominantly about Sarajevo, securing parts of Sarajevo of a majority population, and securing the corridor area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 3, it tasks the 1st Krajina Corps there in the middle of the page to, inter alia, implement offensive actions along the main direction Derventa, Modrica, and Doboj, Podnovlje. Do you see that language?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 09841. This is an order issued by the 1st Krajina Corps shortly thereafter. I'll be asking for page 5 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, here, we see the 1 KK describing its tasks which include, in part, offensive operations using a portion of their forces along the general axes Derventa-Modrica and Doboj-Podnovlje. Do you relate that language to the directive we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's almost a direct lift, and it seems that General Talic has simply taken the instructions he was given in the directive, written his own instructions and passed those down to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we turn back to page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In that first paragraph after the word "enemy," or "neprijatelj," it says in the third line: "Arming of Muslim and Croatian population has already been carried out and they can spring into action at the required moment. All capable of bearing arms are military personnel and they will not refrain from using all available weapons." Do you have any comment on this language?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Talic here is -- is setting out quite an aggressive tone that he believes that anybody who can carry weapons is -- is -- is -- is potentially an enemy. He is not differentiating particularly between those who may be armed or part of an armed organisation, but he is characterising everyone who is capable of carrying weapons as a potential enemy. And this is the kind of command climate or instruction that he is disseminating down to his units. It is not really differentiating at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And is that consistent with what you saw the 1st Krajina Corps and other Bosnian Serb forces doing in the Autonomous Region of Krajina when you reviewed the documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't see too much of a differentiation in the corps, and I know that from, for example, camp documents, the people that they ended up capturing, they would capture people who were not members of the military. So this differentiation I did not think was taken particularly heavily and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09841 receives number P2877, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2877 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 9837.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Traldi kindly speak closer to the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now we see both General Mladic and General Talic's names on this map. What does that signify?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would signify that this was a formal operation that the Main Staff and General Mladic agreed, and clearly it relates to his directive and the fact that both signatures are on it would indicate that there was a commonality of view on how this operation was to be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you, do you really see the signature or just the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's just the block, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. Is there an English translation for the words. Yes, there is. Because we see the -- yes. Yes, I was just wondering what the left top said. But I see in the English translation that it says, "I approve, Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic." Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would object since obviously this is not something that has been worked based on. No signatures. This is -- can be created anywhere at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you tell us where the map comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, my notes say it's from the 1st Krajina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you say, still, forgeries could be in the archives of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this is not a document that anybody worked based on. It would be forbidden to proceed based on the document that is not signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to have it marked for identification for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. There's no claim that on the basis of this, just this map, that one would start any operations. Therefore, that objection is invalid, and the map will be admitted into evidence under number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09837 receives number P2878, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I want to turn now to the discussion of camps that you had mention as moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P377. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you describe what -- the importance of this document for us, briefly, if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This a document that was in the 1st Krajina Corps archive and it's a Main Staff instruction that has been passed down to all the corps to establish prisoners of war camps. At this time Manjaca and the 1st Krajina Corps had already been established but this is a formal instruction to establish camps in other corps. There's a number of handwritten annotations on the side. And it's my assessment that what happened was the 1st Krajina Corps took this Main Staff instruction and General Talic or his staff officers made annotations either in order that a new draft was going to be written for the corps or that he simply just sent this down to the -- his subordinate units. So, for example, there's a handwritten annotation saying, "Assistant commander for moral guidance," who is Colonel Vukelic, "deliver to warden of Manjaca camp. Personally inspect how prisoners of war are being treated." So the annotation is of the 1st Krajina Corps, although the underlying document comes from the Main Staff. There's also an attachment to it which is obligations to -- their obligations to abide by the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you comment at all on the note in the document that there are -- that there are obligations to abide by the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to reinforce that the VRS were aware of the obligations that they -- they had in relation to detainees and prisoners. And they're passing down these instructions down the corps -- down to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the military, what response would you expect to see if orders to follow the law are not obeyed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the military is really actually not any different to -- to anywhere else. If an order is -- military orders and instructions are not obeyed, there should be some kind of sanction -- investigation and sanction and potential punishment if they are not followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you see that response in the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard to what type of activity, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Violations of the instruction here, for instance, to respect the provisions of international laws of war in all treatment of prisoners. We see that just under point 2 on page 1 in both languages. Did you see investigations and prosecutions for that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Have you been able to review the records of the Banja Luka military court at some point --

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, sir, I did. Some time ago now, but we reviewed the records of the court, military court there, and I didn't observe many -- well, there was not investigations and punishments of this type of activity, abuses of detainees. Nor did I actually see other types of activity, including killings or lootings. There were prosecutions of soldiers, disorderly behaviour among themselves, or shooting each other or some other minor disciplinary infractions, but I did not see significant investigations or prosecutions against individuals in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for interpreting an order like this, what does it mean for how subordinate units understand this type of order if it isn't enforced, in the matter you just described?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, discipline is a key function in the military. If you -- if you don't maintain discipline, you can't expect the military to conduct their primary tasks. So if individuals are not punished for infractions like this, the orders become meaningless, on the one hand, and individuals feel that they can get away with such behaviour, and it may lead to an increase in that type of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In your reports, you cite a number of newspaper articles about events in the camps. As far as you could tell, was the 1st Krajina Corps aware of what was being reported about the camps in the international press?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly know of one reference, direct reference to that issue, that what's being reported in the international media is having a detrimental effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did that awareness extend to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the Main Staff were aware of what was happening inside Manjaca. I don't have the daily combat reports of the Main Staff to be able to say that they knew. But I would assume that if that the VRS 1st Krajina Corps were aware of what was happening in the international media, and bearing in mind that the Main Staff had a connection with the RS leadership who were actively involved in negotiations externally, that the VRS Main Staff would be aware of problems in relation to detention camps, especially in July and August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Traldi, I noticed that on the B/C/S version there is some handwriting on the side of the page. I'm not seeing any prevalent translation of that on the English side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you look below the words treatment of prisoners of war, Judge Moloto, Your Honour, I think you will see handwritten in the margin and [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... my apologies. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My understanding is that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the following question to you, Mr. Brown. You were asked about the awareness, whether it extended to the Main Staff. You started saying: "I am aware that the Main Staff were aware of what was happening inside Manjaca." And then you come with a kind of reasoning that they should -- or they would have been aware, but that's not factual knowledge. It's, rather, deduction based partly on assumption. I read the transcript: But I would assume if that the VRS 1st Krajina Corps was aware of what was happening and bearing in mind had a connection with the RS leadership, it's a rather complex type of reasoning rather than a direct conclusion you could draw on the basis of these documents. Would you agree with me that it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have the Main Staff archive and Main Staff documents necessarily that would indicate that. I do know, for example, when Manjaca camp was visited by the ICRC in July, the report that the 1st Krajina Corps made of that visit, which indicated the criticisms that the ICRC had, was communicated to the Main Staff. And that was a document sent on the 16th of July. And, in fact, that document arrived at the Main Staff before the Karadzic instruction enclosing the ICRC report. So that is one reference that I do know that the VRS Main Staff received from the 1st Krajina Corps outlining the problems that the ICRC -- significant problems that the ICRC had observed in that camp in the middle of July. There are --

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that is -- that is one aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we might, Your Honour, just call up P230. I believe that next document is the one Mr. Brown is describing so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But, nevertheless, Mr. Brown, I listen carefully to your first line of the answer of my question. You say: "Yes. I don't have the Main Staff archives and Main Staff documents necessarily that would indicate that."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also could have said, I don't have the Main Staff archive and Main Staff documents, so I do not know whether they indicate awareness. You see the difference in your phrase and in my phrase. Your phrase is more or less starting, I don't have the evidence from what I know was the case. I say, I don't have the evidence; therefore, I wouldn't know, at least what the content of that evidence would have been. Could I invite you to be very strict in this respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not to say, I don't have it so that's the reason I can't prove it. If I would have it the evidence would be there. Because if you don't have the evidence, then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it may be further open. I just wanted to let you know that I carefully listened to not only to the content of your testimony but also to the language you are using.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have P230, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly requesting the witness to speak into the microphones again, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is this the document you were referring to just a moment ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you see it's -- it's sent to the Main Staff of the army and to the Doboj operations group?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any action in response from the Main Staff around this time, 16 July 1992, in your review of the documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any instructions in the Krajina Corps archive coming down to the -- to the corps making significant -- asking for significant changes on the basis of this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 06982.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's an order from General Mladic several weeks later.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an instruction later, but I believe that was on the basis of the Karadzic request later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We can call those up in just a moment, sir. This document under the words, "I order," on page 1 says: "Immediately undertake measures through the MUP and authorities to arrange POW camps in your zones of responsibility and prepare them for visits by foreign journalists and International Red Cross team." Can you tell us what has been happening in that regard based on the documents you reviewed between 16 July and 3 August?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been, after the ICRC visit, some articles that had appeared in the media by Roy Gutman at the end of August. Concurrently with this, there were negotiations ongoing in London. And it would seem from this -- these negotiations that the issue of camps had arisen and that agreement had been given for foreign journalists to visit these camps in early August, most likely in reaction to the criticisms that Gutman, for example, had written about in relation to the detention centres in the Krajina. So here we have a Main Staff instruction coming down indicating that these visits are to be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The document refers to a plan to visit camps including Omarska, Trnopolje and Manjaca. Did journalists visit camps around this time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how did that go?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would argue that far from, if you like, identifying that these institutions were -- were favourable, they actually made the situation or they portrayed the situation that they were -- they were -- they were poor locations and the situation was made worse in a way for the Serbs by those visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Brown, you're saying at page 44, line 16: "There were poor locations and the situation was made worse for the Serbs by those visits."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe it's a -- certainly -- maybe not the best expression. I think in order to placate the criticisms that were happening at the end of August, this visit was allowed. And on the 5th, the journalists visited the camps, but they reported that they were, in essence, in an even worse condition or that the situation was worse than -- than -- in the past. So rather than defusing the situation by the visit, it actually opened up the camps, further opened up the camps to international -- to the international media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06982 receives number P2879, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could I ask you the following, Mr. Brown: We looked earlier at the report about the ICRC visit which you said demonstrated that the Main Staff had awareness of what happened in Manjaca camp. Now, the criticism contained in that report, would you agree with me that that certainly not covers all the things that may have happened in those camps? It only partially addresses what is addressed by evidence this Chamber heard about how people were transported to the camps and how people were -- died during those events. Hardly anything of that kind appears in the reporting on the basis of the ICRC visit. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it possible for me to see the document again, the one that went to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was -- was it P230, Mr. Traldi or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are two, actually, and I might ask which would assist more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16th of July. That was one the one I had on my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: P230 then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is by far earlier than the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you need to look at the second page, don't hesitate to ask, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second page would be useful, sir. Could we go back to the first page again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could I ask you already about the second page. That would be my second question. Whether the report reflects all the things this Chamber heard evidence about, that is, killing, et cetera, whether, in page 2, there are several reasons reported to the Main Staff explaining that the dissatisfaction is not due to the condition in the camps but that other reasons are given for the dissatisfaction of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would argue, sir, that the -- the -- the criticisms on page 1 are significant. If we could go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you also -- first respond to my second question, whether, on page 2, main reasons are given --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- why it is not the conditions in the camp but for other reasons that the ICRC is dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The -- the -- the author gives his reasons as why these criticisms are not justified and so -- so in that respect, that is the case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that was reported to the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was reported to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are back at page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the criticisms that are reported from the ICRC that are reported to the Main Staff are that there's a lack of food, loss of weight of prisoners, risk of epidemic, that they -- I believe earlier on that they hadn't been allowed to see certain individuals. The health of the problem -- of the -- of the prisoners. And, I believe, that there -- fresh traces of -- of blood in the camps on the prisoners. Now, reading this, I -- I think that these are quite significant criticisms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether these are significant criticisms. My question was, talking about awareness of what happened in Manjaca camp, whether this report also includes other events the Chamber heard evidence about, that is about killing. I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay, I understand. I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if blood is found somewhere, that doesn't mean that someone is killed yet. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... of course. No, of course, sir. No, it doesn't mention killings in this report. It does allude to some of the other poor conditions that are there, however. Maybe that's my point, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the awareness, if it would have to be based on this document, would be partially only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On those issues. Maybe this is not a -- part of your -- I will -- I will leave it. I was going to deal with something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 03326, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I add why I asked this question, because you -- I gained the impression that you jumped rather quickly to conclusions as the Main Staff was aware on what happened in Manjaca camp, where the reporting certainly does not cover everything we heard about [Overlapping speakers] ... so a more cautious conclusion would have been appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree, sir. There is a reference obviously in early August when the Omarska prisoners arrived at Manjaca that there were deaths during the transportation. That was in a daily combat report that went to the Main Staff. But based on this document, sir, I wholeheartedly agree. It doesn't reference specifically killings. It does certainly allude to me that the conditions in these other areas are being reported by the ICRC and that the Main Staff is being made aware of these criticisms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this document begins on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to intervene for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After your question from line 6 to line 10, on page 48, witness twice said "I agree, Your Honour." Actually, "I agree, sir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're right. The witness expressed that he agreed in those respects with my observations. We'll move on. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This document here, sir, we see: "Dear Mr. Prime Minister, I hereby deliver to you copies of the reports on the situation in Manjaca and Bileca prisons that I just received. In regard to these reports, I have sent a letter to Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga, the president of ICRC, and to General Ratko Mladic." At the bottom of the page, we see, again, Mr. Karadzic's stamp and signature. Could we turn to page 5 in the English and in the B/C/S. And here we see the Red Cross report. And it notes here, under point 2: "All eight delegates present in camp observed on detainees frequent and widespread traces of recent and often severe beatings; these most often were fresh hematomas inflicted in a time-period since arrival at Manjaca." Does this document also contribute to the conclusion you were just expressing that the Main Staff was aware of the ICRC findings in this respect?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this would seem to be a very critical report of the conditions that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 6 of the English and 7 in the B/C/S, just under the words "ICRC recommends that," towards the top of the page, the first sentence we see is: "Manjaca camp is not suitable for detention and should be closed ..." Do you have any comment on that language, sir?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- it says what it is, and it's the recommendation that a prestigious organisation that is involved in this type of work and monitoring globally the conditions in detention camps. It is recommending that Manjaca camp is not suitable for -- for detention and should be closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered this document.
