utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03326 receives number P2880, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Could we go back to the first page of this document. Mr. Brown, the last sentence in the very short letter on page 1 of this document, a letter by Radovan Karadzic, refers to: "Living conditions in the prisons on our territories that are being held by civil authorities." Do you have any comment on this reference to the civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly what Karadzic is meaning by "civil authorities" or whether he is talking about military authorities within that umbrella, whether he is talking about any prison camps seems slightly ambiguous, but there is an emphasis to try and make the conditions better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I see that. But my focus was on that Mr. Karadzic expects the government to take prompt action through the Ministries of Justice and Interior. Apparently not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the military. And clearly points at the civil authorities - and that's how I read this line - being competent to deal with the conditions in those camps. And I'm asking your comment on that specific aspect of this correspondence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I'm not sure I can add too much more than you've explained, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't explained anything. I just read what I saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not sure I can add anything there. There is an omission there of the Ministry of Defence or the Main Staff in -- bearing in mind Manjaca was a military camp. But it does seem that Karadzic is requesting prompt action to make these camps -- or improve these camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it your view in the context of all of the documents that Mr. Karadzic rightly qualifies the camps as being held by civil authorities, or would you consider this to be not in the context of all the documentary evidence a right qualification of the -- of who is holding those camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- obviously the civil authorities are the ones he talks about, but it's not exactly clear what he is referring to there, so I'm not sure I can add too much more, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I understand civil authorities not to be the authorities in the military line of command and control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Normally that would be the case, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there any reason to understand it in any different way than here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which would mean that the Main Staff had no role to play here. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I think the -- the language, to me, is somewhat ambiguous. I'm not sure clearly what he means. From my experience as a military officer, if the military are holding individuals in a detention camp, it is their responsibility. And it's their responsibility for the conditions and, as far as I am aware, on international law. So I can't necessarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it that you don't know what he means, or is it that you think that this language conceals the military role in holding the -- for example, the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine that it's whoever is running the facilities that they're running, and that's what he means. Civil authorities meaning if there's a police camp, it is run by them; or if it's a military camp, it's run by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what about the two mentioned in view of the documents you studied? Manjaca and Bileca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they're military-run facility, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you say is you disagree with this qualification by Karadzic that these are prisons held by civil authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are camps run by the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, not being held by civil authorities. That's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question. At the end of the first paragraph of this letter, there's a reference that Mr. Karadzic has sent a letter to the president of the ICRC and to General Ratko Mladic. During your study of documents, have you seen this letter to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your understanding of this reference to a letter sent by Karadzic to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, is it possible to go to the next -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think attached there's only the report by ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I haven't seen a copy of the letter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And maybe just to follow up on some of Your Honours' questions before we break, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: By your understanding, who was the commander of Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bozidar Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps, Commander General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Talic's chain of command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we slow down, even if the answers need less thinking, that we take a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think, in fact, Your Honour, probably because I had failed to do that, the witness's answer at line 24 wasn't recorded, so I'll ask more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was Colonel Popovic's chain of command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He reported to General Talic, commander of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to whom did General Talic report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Talic reported to the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to follow up on His Honour Judge Fluegge's question, could we have 65 ter 00640.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the top here under the words "improvement of the accommodation of the POWs," it says: "The Presidency of SRBiH sent us a written report on the state of POWs in the camp on Mount Manjaca made by the International Committee of Red Cross during their visit to the said camp on 17 July 1992." Does that inform your view as to whether the Main Staff received the information contained in the document we just saw assigned by Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to see that the Main Staff received that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tendered this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 00640 receives number P2881, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, we take a break, and could you tell us after the break how much - let's do it in minutes - you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just note that there have been questions from the Bench this session - that's because of the importance of the material, of course - and so it will be no more than half the session, but maybe half the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take a break after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I've just a few more questions about the detention camps, sir. Conscious of the dates in those few documents we just looked at as being July and August of 1992, were there large-scale releases of detainees from Manjaca around that time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documents that I was able to see, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in, for instance, paragraph 2.130 of your Krajina report, you discuss that no significant release of prisoners from Manjaca was carried out until November of 1992 and the majority in December. What do you take from that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bearing in mind that a number of the Manjaca camp reports themselves indicated that there were large numbers of individuals who they deemed didn't deserve to be there and a corps reference to the same thing in August, and bearing in mind the criticisms that had come out from the ICRC, the camps that -- -- they were not released for some number of months in the -- till winter of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour I won't show them at this point but I would refer the Chamber, for instance, to Exhibits P220 and 221.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, on the occasions that those large releases took place, in November and December 1992, were prisoners returned home?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the documents that I saw, the prisoners were moved and bussed into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And was the Main Staff informed of those deportations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The daily combat reports in December, in particular, referenced the moving out of the detainees and the closure of the camp in that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 06003, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a 1st Krajina report dated the 14th of December, 1992. Under point 3, on page 1 in both languages, we say -- we read, rather: "The release of prisoners of war from Manjaca is proceeding as planned, noting the following: At 1555 hours a convoy of buses with 1.008 prisoners crossed the Sava river bridge in Gradiska." Is this an example of what you were just discussing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were two large movements around this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tendered 65 ter 06003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06003 receives number P2882, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2882 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: To go back to August for a moment, in your reports you describe the process the Republika Srpska government went through regarding the camps at that time, and you described the process as a whitewash. Can you just explain the basis for your conclusion in that regard.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the media interest in the camps and the -- the -- the international response to that, the Bosnian Serbs did in -- conduct their own investigation into the camps and the report there seems to be marked -- difference to the ICRC report. The ICRC report was, as we've seen, very critical of the camp and recommended that it was closed. That didn't happen for a long -- quite a long time. And individuals who the camp documents, camp records identified as, in essence, having nothing to do with the conflict were detained for a significantly large amount of time in a location that the ICRC had clearly condemned. That's not what the Bosnian Serb report said, and they did not close the camp on the basis of the ICRC report in July. It was some significant time after this that the individuals were -- were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Speaking of camps now generally not just Manjaca but the others that you saw discussed in those Bosnian Serb documents to which you were just referring, in any of those documents did you see any clear reference that anyone was punished for what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the records that I saw. And certainly I saw no senior officer or officer at all being investigated or held to account for any of the allegations that were identified in those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to turn to what happened to those non-Serbs who were not taken to camps. Starting in paragraph 2.187 of your Krajina report, you describe what you term follow-on operations. And earlier you described the consequences of the operations in late May for non-Serb communities. Do we see the same types of consequences for these follow-on operations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going turn now to one of the last operations in the ARK in the village of Vecici. I'm going to show you three documents and then ask you some questions. The first is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff on 2 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 16537, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As this comes up, can you tell us about the context of what is happening in and around Vecici at the time.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the document I reviewed from the corps there had been operations in the summer in Kotor Varos, but, in essence, the last area that had not been taken under control by the Bosnian Serb forces was the area of Vecici which did have a non-component, I believe, and there were some operations that were being launched out of that area. But, in essence, it was an area, one of the last pockets in that municipality, that the Serbs did not control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 of the English on this first document but stay on page 1 of the B/C/S. Under point 3, it reads: "In the Kotor Varos area (village of Vecici) negotiations about the disarming of the extremists who have barricaded themselves continue. There have been no significant occurrences in other parts of the territory." Again, the date, 2 November. Could we have 65 ter 02617, please. These are a collection of minutes of the Kotor Varos War Presidency in late October and early November of 1992. On page 1 here, under point 2, we see that President Djekanovic said that Colonel Bogojevic would come during the day and that any -- and that Mladic had ordered that any agreement with him regarding Vucic - we'll check the translation, but I believe that should be "Vecici" - should be implemented. If we turn to page 3, please. At the top here we see a list of attendees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brown, can you just help us as to a few of the players. What is Colonel Bogojevic's role at this time?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bogojevic is the chief of security at the 1st Krajina Corps, assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Major Trivic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm assume they are referring to Major Janko Trivic, who was operations group Vlasic commander. That was an operational group that covered the area of a number of municipalities, Kotor Varos being one of them. And it was a subordinate formation of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- Novakovic is the commander of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then we see a note from Colonel Bogojevic informing all present that he had received explicit orders from General Mladic that no one was to be allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of weapons was completed. What conclusion do you draw from these two documents about General Mladic's involvement in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear that -- that General Mladic is actively aware of what is happening in Vecici and has issued instructions to senior officer in the corps that -- that there has to be an unconditional surrender in the area, so he is obviously well-known, well versed what was happening, and he is taking it upon himself to send down a senior officer from the corps in order to ensure that that message is passed down to the -- the local actors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript is not very clear, but it is my recollection that you said that there has to be an unconditionally surrender in the area. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think is unconditional surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know whether you said that but I missed the word of "weapons." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender those two documents; first, 16537.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 16537 receives P2883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And second, 02617.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02617 receives number P2884, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I have to decide on admission. I see we have 2887 and then 2884. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 16537 should receive number P2883. And then document 02617 should receive number P2884, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then 2883 and 2884 are admitted into evidence. And what I said about 2887 is vacated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 2939, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is another 1st Krajina Corps report to the Main Staff dated 3 November. And we see here towards the bottom of point 1, first page both languages: "During the night, armed soldiers left the village of Vecici for an unknown destination, and civilians holding a white flag are walking in a column toward the village of Vrbanjci." And I think I may have mispronounced the second village. Does this support your conclusion as to the level of information the Main Staff was receiving about events there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Staff is being informed about the operation in that area in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered 65 ter 02939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02939 receives number P2885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2885 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P441. This is another report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, again, I'll show you two documents and ask you afterwards for your expert conclusion. This document states under point 2 in both languages, second paragraph: "In the area of Kotor Varos, there was a clash between members of Muslim forces and our units" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'll do so more slowly, Mr. President: "Because of the refusal to negotiate on moving out of the Vecici village area, about 40 Green Berets members were killed and about 200 were captured. A brutal massacre of the captured Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade, and the burning of wounded soldiers at a place in Jajce." Could we have P442, please. This will be another report from the 1st Krajina Corps to the Main Staff the next day. And it comes up I'll be looking at point 4 on page 1 in both languages. In the second paragraph it reads: "In the clash --" sorry, I should start at the first: "The situation in the Kotor Varos municipality is still very complex. After they refused to return the weapons and surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska, Muslim extremists from the village of Vecici attempted to fight their way towards Travnik. "In the clash against the Army of Republika Srpska, following the death of one soldier and the wounding of several others, more than 150 extremists died in combat."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What do you take from these two documents?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document it is quite a -- slightly more detailed in relating the story that there have been some casualties but the captured have been killed in a brutal massacre, as a result, in essence, of a revenge attack because of the deaths of individuals within the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade. The following day those casualties seemed to be portrayed as combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you have any view on that evolution?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would seem to be indicating that there had been a criminal act, and the other one that these casualties were acceptable and combat casualties and ... they've changed the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P356, page 121 in both languages. This will be another of General Mladic's notebooks. It's possible, based on the right diagram, that my notes are in error. Could we go forward a page, please. Here, this records a meeting -- we don't have the B/C/S yet, so actually I'll pause for a moment. I believe it should be the same page in the B/C/S as the English. And now we have it. This records a meeting General Mladic attends in Banja Luka with senior officers in the 1st Krajina Corps on 2 November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you review General Mladic's notebooks for the period related to the Vecici documents we've just discussed, the 2nd through the 5th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did recently, and General Mladic is in Banja Luka and the Krajina area in those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say the Krajina area, within either the 1st or 2nd Krajina Corps' area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And how does that impact your view on the documents we just looked at regarding Vecici?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may give some context as to why General Mladic's name is in the instructions in the -- the -- the -- the minutes of the meeting and why a senior officer from the corps has been sent down. It would seem that General Mladic is in the area meeting with the corps commander, and maybe that is one of the reasons why the -- General Mladic's instructions are being -- are being heeded. It certainly would seem to shorten the chain of command if he is physically present meeting with the Krajina Corps officers on the 2nd of November, the same day that the security chief is sent down by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 03921, please. This is the 1st Krajina Corps' 1993 report on combat readiness in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, can you tell us something about what this document is.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document compiled by the Main Staff in spring of 1993, in essence, as a reflection on what it had achieved in the previous period and also as a mechanism of identifying any weaknesses and looking ahead as to what they were to do. So it is a reflective document as much as it is about looking forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You referred to the Main Staff combat readiness report. Were there corps reports prepared that went into the preparation of that report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, sir. And the 1st Krajina Corps compiled their only analysis report which would have formed one of the underlying documents needed to compile this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just for the clarity of the transcript, could you perhaps review the page and tell us which one we're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1st Krajina Corps's combat readiness report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to page 12 in the English and on page 17 in the B/C/S, towards the bottom in the English. It reads, "We achieved" -- if we could scroll down a little so we have the whole relevant language: "We achieved significant results in activities related to prisoner of war exchanges. Within the 1st Krajina Corps' zone, over 9.200 prisoners were exchanged, of which 2.300 were military personnel from the former BH, plus the bodies of around 250 individuals who were killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you have any comment on this language?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seemed to indicate that they've taken a significant number -- or exchanged a significant number of prisoners, and they've certainly divided military personnel from the former BH as a category from that, leaving the remainder presumably were not personnel, military personnel from the former BH. But it certainly identifies that they'd taken a large number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what's reflected there, roughly 25 per cent, I think, of the prisoners, they reflect as exchanged being military personnel?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the former BH, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: From the former BH. Is that roughly consistent -- not specific numbers, obviously, but is that surprising to you based on the documents you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's surprising in the terms of the size of numbers or the content?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The ratio of military personnel to total prisoners.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is small. It's more than I'd expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you assess the Main Staff's level of awareness of what the 1st Krajina Corps was doing in 1992 based on the process reflected in this document as well as the daily reporting you've described earlier?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 1st Krajina Corps was keeping the Main Staff informed through its daily combat reports from the moment of its transition. In fact, there was a seamless transition, really. It was a professional corps. From the document that I reviewed, from the archive, it kept the Main Staff and recognised that it had to keep the Main Staff informed, both through the daily combat reports and then obviously in a document like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tendered 65 ter 03921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03921 receives number P2886, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2886 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document I'd ask for is the one that I'd referred to yesterday where we've sought to add it to the 65 ter list. 65 ter 30391 has been provisionally assigned. It's an excerpt from General Talic's personnel file that reflects an assessment by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And contains how many pages? How long is it? And what is the reason why? Oversight?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The English translation was only requested over the summer, and we disclosed it to the Defence as soon as we identified it and sought to add it a couple of weeks, I think, after we had had a chance to review the English version. It's about two, three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We already objected to this. We already objected to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You already objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants leave to have it added to the 65 ter list and overrules the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask for it to be called up then. As usual, by the time I ask for it, it's already happening. So we see General Talic's name here on the first page. Can we turn to page 2 in both languages, please. Sorry, page 2 in the B/C/S but page 3 in the English. I won't read the whole evaluation, but I'm starting at the fourth line in the English on page 3: "After it's withdrawal of the JNA from BH, together with his associates, he successfully, and in a very short period, set up the 1st Krajina Corps" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're reading, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President: "... which was the strike force of the VRS, and he successfully conducted the battles for the liberation of Posavina and other Serbian areas." It discusses more details below that and then concludes: "He receives the grade of excellent."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you hadn't seen this document when you prepared your reports. Have you reviewed it in preparation for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed this a couple of days ago. It was the first time I had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you have any comment on what we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of things, I guess. One is that the corps had conducted its operations, such as Operation Corridor in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Guessing is not what we expect anyone to do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, it's a phrase. General Mladic is congratulating or making a reference that the 1st Krajina Corps, under Talic's command, has successfully achieved the objectives set: Operation Corridor which was a strategic objective and the liberation of its territory in its zone. And he has given an excellent grade. There aren't any references or criticisms of any of the activity in which his corps was involved in. There are no criticisms of operations against -- that resulted in civilian deaths. None of the retaliatory actions which are referenced in my report, none of the issues relating to the camp which sat under his authority. So General Talic is given an excellent grade, which I find knowing what his corps had been involved in somewhat -- somewhat of note. That despite all the issues that I referenced in my report he was still given an excellent grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 30391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are now at the stage of admission or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection to admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30391 receives number P2887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2887 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then the last document I'll show you, sir, is one that you mentioned before, just a couple of moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P338. And I'd request page 159 in the English; 138 in the B/C/S. This is the Main Staff combat readiness report for 1992 drafted in 1993. Looking at the second paragraph in the English, fourth line, the language I want to point you to reads: "The strategic objectives of our war which were promptly defined and set before the Main Staff of the Army of RS, the commands and units, served as a general guide-line upon which we planned the actual operations and concerted battles." That's at the bottom of the page in B/C/S or towards it. It continues a couple of lines thereafter, turning to the next page in the B/C/S: "The Main Staff of the Army of RS translated the set objectives and tasks into general an individual missions of the Army of RS and of the individual operational and tactical formations with the goals of every individual combat action, operation, or battle being specifically defined."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What does this language signify, in your view?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would seem to echo what I was discussing earlier that there were political and strategic goals given by the leadership and that the Main Staff took those and used them as the formation of their operations which they disseminated down to the corps, and they -- they were -- so that effective chain of command functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 160 now in the English. It sets out some of the objectives that we've just been discussing. It says at the very top: "The primary focus for the Army of RS for quite some time had been to open and maintain a corridor linking the Republic of Serbian Krajina through the Bosnian Krajina with Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Does that relate, in your view, to the corridor operation we've discussed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that reflects Karadzic's statement at the 16th Assembly Session, the operation in June and the operation that the 1st Krajina Corps was successful in during the summer months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the end of that same paragraph, it continues: "In the last month and a half, our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje, as thereby the strategic objective of our war would be realised, one that could be defined as 'establishing contact' with Serbia on the river Drina, or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier." Do you also relate that to one of the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's strategic objective 3, and it very much mirrors the language of Karadzic at the 16th Assembly Session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Have you reviewed -- actually, you discuss in your statement documents related to directive 4. Does that relate to this Podrinje area?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does give tasks to other corps, but the emphasis very much is on the Podrinje area and that was around November --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. In -- in this document, second paragraph, it reads: "The presence of the commander of the Main Staff, or of a representative of the Main Staff, in the units carrying out the mission of the liberation of Podrinje is a specific way of giving weight to and steering combat operations towards a single goal." Based on your review of directive 4 and the associated documents, can you comment on what that single goal was?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the single goal is the goal articulated in the -- in strategic goal number 3, which is to secure the Drina -- corridor in the Drina, eliminating the border between Serbia and RS territory. And that is echoed in the tasks that were given to that corps, the Drina Corps in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What place -- based on your review of directive 4 and the related documents, what place was contemplated for the non-Serb population in the Podrinje area after that goal or in the implementation of that goal?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember of the directive, and I'm -- it was that the Muslim population were to be driven out. I mean, it may not be the exact language, I would have to go back to the document, but I believe that's the -- the emphasis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you relate that goal to the operations that you saw or that you reviewed in the ARK?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I relate that goal to the issue of strategic goal number 1, as much as the Drina valley being secured and that of the separation of communities. So I -- I relate it to as much to strategic goal number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, I suggest that we take a little bit longer break, 25 minutes, and then have a last session of 1 hour and 20 minutes, so moving up to quarter to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we start, I -- just for the record, I was warned by Ms. Registrar that probably I misspoke on 8th November, 2013, on page 19040, line 1 to line 16, on the same page. It is wrongly recorded doc ID number. It -- it was recorded 1D06-1678, and it should be corrected, and correct number is 1D07-0678. And it's English translation of the document D389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you corrected, Mr. Lukic. I can't say from the top of my head now the problem is resolved, but it's on the record at least now, and whomever has to work with it is now put on notice that they should read this as well, and not only the 8th of November transcript. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready. Mr. Brown, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your report? We'll be using first Krajina report, P2859.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in front of me, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this -- this morning I gave copies for Your Honours of this report, so we don't have to flip in between the report and the documents, and you can follow the whole paragraphs. Maybe I could miss something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I always have some concerns because of the paper spent but because I have it on my screen as well. Let's proceed and we appreciate your efforts to make life easier for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, in your report, this will be page 5 in English and in B/C/S, we can see a summary. In the summary, in the first paragraph, it says in the last sentence: "By April 1992, there had been a growing convergence between the JNA and the Serbian Democratic Party."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same report, in paragraph 1.3, i.e., in the first part dealing with the political and military situation, I repeat, paragraph 1.3, you quote a JNA document -- or you, rather, cite it. And you say in that quote that the HDZ, the SDA and the SDS effectively created all the necessary conditions in terms of the economy, politics, and military conditions in order to launch armed conflicts and to put up armed resistance against the JNA. This is relative to a document which was produced in January 1995 [as interpreted]. My question, sir, is this: Did you come across a document which describes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting Mr. Lukic. But he's described the document as produced in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1992, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the document was created in January 1992. In your work, did you come across any paper trail of a pronounced discord between the SDS and the JNA? Even in the months of April and May, up to the very end, up to the moment when the JNA finally drew -- withdrew, all that time, there was a lack of trust between the two, between the SDS and the JNA. Did you come across any documents that speak about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you refer the witness to paragraph 1.3. Do I understand you to be referring to paragraph 1.3 at page 21 of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you can give us page numbers whenever you refer to paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the page is labelled as 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Twelve, exactly, not 21. I -- it's paragraph 1-3, 1.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come across any evidence to the fact that there was no trust between the SDS and the JNA, even in the months of April and May of that year?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't see that lack of trust, certainly in the latter part in April and May, because there were meetings between Mr. Karadzic and others in the early days of -- of May. So, at the earlier period, no. This document that you refer to is dated well before that. I can't remember ever single footnote because it's been some time since I've gone through all the documents but it may be that this document is a reflection back on 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, I said it was from January 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's from January 1991, but I think it is referring to the situation a little bit earlier than that. But irrespective, what I saw in the early months certainly were criticisms of the SDS and other parties by the JNA in the early months of 1992. But my report, I believe, argues that there became a convergence between the two certainly in the months of spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will make short breaks for the benefit of the interpreters who are interpreting all of our words and they need time to do that. Did you come across any documents that showed that the SDS armed some formations and the reason was that they did not trust the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report was not to look at whether the SDS armed or the functions of the SDS, but I do know that there are some references -- at least I can remember one specific reference in March 1992 which the JNA make note of weapons that have been distributed to volunteers and it references arms that have been given to the SDS. Whether the SDS were arming, I'm sure they were. But it wasn't really the function of this report to look into the details of whether the SDS were arming in the early part of 1992 or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the Serbian Defence forces whose abbreviation was SOS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was their leader? Do you know that? Who was in command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was a leader, but I do know that Stevandic, Nenad Stevandic was a member. It's a name I remember. I'm not sure if it's a leader. There is a reference I also know in one of the VRS documents which dealt with paramilitaries that makes mention of the SOS. I also know that around the time of the discussions about what was happening to the JNA in April 1992 that the SOS were pretty unhappy that the JNA may be leaving. But the SOS was not an organisation I specifically looked into in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you actually agree with me that both Muslims and Croats pushed the JNA towards the Serbs by attacking them in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "Muslims and Croats"? Are you meaning all of them or -- can you -- can you qualify the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It will become clear from the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19649 is the document that I would like to call up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, let me tell you that the document was apparently issued by the Territorial Defence Staff of the Ministry for National Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. It was issued on the 29 April 1992. And it is says on the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- I have no objection to the document being used. I would suggest that for full context, adjudicated fact 853, which is related, also be put to the witness. And I'll leave it at that, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you follow that suggestion, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd be happy to provided it to him after he's read his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had some suggestions that Mr. Traldi follows my wishes during his direct. Now I leave it to him for his re-direct. If he has -- wants to use something I'll happily leave it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters short. If you want to -- put it as you wish. Mr. Traldi thought it would save time to put it directly in a broader context. But if -- if you don't follow his suggestion, which was the only thing I asked you, then Mr. Traldi will, in re-examination, I take it, deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I will. I put on that I think the witness may be given an incomplete picture of the evidence [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: About the [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is on the record. And, Mr. Lukic, of course the Chamber expects you to proceed in a way which is both in the interests of the Defence but also not to waste time or to -- and I do not know whether it would mislead the witness, but if it would, of course, you should refrain from it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope I had not mislead the witness and I don't think that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... presenting the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed as you deem fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order on the implementation of a decision by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the number is also mentioned, the number of that decision. It says: "Pursuant to the decision of 27 April 1992 issued by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina pertaining to the retreat of the JNA units from the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and due to this decision by the Presidency not being implemented and due to the fact that the appropriation and theft of property of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is carried out by the former JNA." It says, "I hereby order." Under number 1 it says, "Carry out a full and large-scale prevention on all roads" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page in English. We are by now. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Complete various systems are to be set up along the routes on the territory of the Bosnia and Herzegovina along which the former JNA units start extracting technical and materiel equipment. This is to be done in direct co-ordination with the MUP." Under 4, it says: Speed up the planning of combat activities and launch combat activities as soon as possible on the whole territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those are to be co-ordinated with the Territorial Defence Staff at the regional, district, and national levels in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did you have this document in your hands? Did you review it? The document was sent by the then-minister of defence, Mr. Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have this document at hand, and I haven't reviewed it until you showed it to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would this document have influenced your conclusions as to who the JNA sided with?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document wouldn't have changed the conclusions. It seems to be contextually in terms of its timing, of importance, and in terms of the content, it would seem to be doing two things. One is stopping the JNA from removing property that the republic believes is theirs; and, as you note, on 4, planning for combat operations is to be speeded up. The timing of this document is late; in fact very late April. It's not an area of my expertise necessarily that I have reviewed, but it would seem that there had already been significant activity in locations like Bijeljina and Zvornik and also in Sarajevo which might have been the reason for this issuance of the planning for combat operations. But it -- it doesn't add or change my view that, by this time, this convergence was very much apparent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You dealt with various municipalities in Krajina, including, Prijedor, for example. Do you know what effect this document had on the take-over of power in Prijedor? Did you learn why the SDS took over power in Prijedor? Do you know that the reason was that by mistake this document ended up in the Serbian hands as well, but it was by mistake that it happened?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that it was -- it was made by mistake ending up in Serbian hands at all. I didn't know that. What I do know is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Lukic, it would help us if you would announce that you would consult with your client so that we could ask the witness to stop answering the question and that not any of the evidence is lost for you. Could I ask the witness to resume from where Mr. Lukic left us. You said: "I wasn't a ware that it was ... made by mistake ending up in Serbian hands ..." And then you told us what you do know. Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know that around this time in late April, the SDS took control of the municipality of Prijedor, and that included the engagement of Vladimir Arsic, a JNA officer, in that -- in that -- at this time. But I can't tell you about the activities with this document and its impact in Prijedor. If you -- if your position is that this is the document that sparks off the municipality take-overs, I would just point out that there were municipalities other than Prijedor that had already been taken over by the SDS, including Bratunac and Zvornik, well before this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In view of the documents that have been tendered, are you testifying about Podrinje or about Krajina? What is your report about? If you're testifying about Podrinje, I'm prepared to go there as well, but I have to know.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my report is about the Krajina. But clearly there are other areas that would have -- that I'm aware of. But the report itself deals with the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19649 receives number D41, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D41 would surprise me, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D412 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at the following document, 1D1460, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Traldi, you have posed the Chamber for quite a bit of a puzzle in relation to this report, and I didn't want to address it until I thought I would know what the puzzle was approximately about. I think all the attached versions to the 92 bis notice and the -- 94 bis notice and the 92 ter motion are a version of the report "Military developments in the Bosanska Krajina," which is dated the 27th of November. However, in your 94 bis notice, you referred to 65 ter 11329, and if you would look under that number, you suddenly find a different version of the report in English, which is a 21st of July, 2002, version of the same report, although the translation attached in B/C/S is, again, the 27th of November report. So when I earlier said that I could look at my electronic version, I suddenly found out it is not exactly the same as the one provided to us at many occasions by the Prosecution and by Mr. Lukic. Do you have any solution for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears there is a clerical error in the text of the notice. The version that was attached on both occasions is the version that I asked to have marked for identification yesterday. That's the 27 November. I believe that's the version Mr. Lukic -- well, I haven't been provided with what he provided you, but if it is page 12, then that's the version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 27th of November. Nevertheless, the 65 ter number you referred to in your 94 bis motion is about the same report, but a different version. And then, of course, it comes as a surprise to find that the English -- apart from whether we should uses it or not, the English of 65 ter 11329 is the July report; whereas the B/C/S is the November report, which is -- is clearly some kind of a mistake. I do understand we work exclusively on the basis of the 27th of November report of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's the report we've requested admission for, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is 65 ter 11012 MFI'd now as P2859. Let's proceed but I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D1460.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that some municipalities had already been taken over. However, this document will show that Muslim attacks had also started much earlier. In this document, which was issued on the 19th of April, 1992, General Kukanjac addresses President Alija Izetbegovic. The document says that in the course of the night of April 17 through 18, 1992, your Green Berets have carried out an attack on part of a factory in Vogosca, which is Pretis. And then there was an attack in Konjic in the course of the night of April 18th through 19. Further on, it says everything is blocked. All telephones of the PTT been turned off. The Green Berets have occupied the military equipment factory in Malin Konjic. Military medical vehicles are held, searched, and the personnel is ill-treated. Food for the soldiers has not been delivered. And further on, General Kukanjac asks President Izetbegovic to call off his forces so that they stopped attacking JNA forces. On the following page in the B/C/S version, and the same page in English, it says: "Do not forget that we have signed a peace agreement on April 12, 1992. And on that same day" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go back to the earlier page, please. Sorry, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English, it's previous page, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Kukanjac warns, and he says: "Do not forget that we signed a peace agreement on April 12, 1992, and that on that very same day you issued that famous directive of yours by way of which you declare a war against the JNA, against Serbs and other innocent citizens." Putting that directive out of force is nothing but a farce, but a charade. All actions by the SDA and those armies of yours show that you opted for war. In your review of the documents, did you come across this specific document issued by the SDA and Alija Izetbegovic which declared a war on the JNA on the 12th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that document on the 12th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you had known about this document which is before us and other documentation that speaks about it, would you have changed your position about the bias held by the JNA? Would you accept that the JNA was impartial until the moment when the Muslim armed forces started attacking it openly?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wouldn't change the underlying assertion in this report. I acknowledge in the report that the JNA were in a difficult position and that also the JNA were attacked in some areas. I think I make mention in the report to the corridor, for example. My report indicates that the JNA wished to see Bosnia remain part of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So it was in its interests for that to happen. But my report also highlights some documentation that the JNA were distributing and siding more and more with the SDS, the Bosnian Serbs, and the SDS's position through the spring of 1992. I don't doubt that there were attacks on the JNA, but it doesn't change my underlying assertion that there was a convergence between the JNA and the SDS in those months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your work, did you observe any orchestrated use of the armed forces of the Muslim element in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can really only talk about the area of the Krajina in -- in detail, although I'm aware of some areas outside of that, but the report deals with the -- with the Krajina. Can you be more specific in relation to that? Are you asking me ... in -- in that area?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We'll come --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that. But, Mr. Lukic, you're not interested in an answer to your last question, which was not very precise to me, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have -- let me use another document to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For the orchestrated use of the armed forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't entirely clear to me. No objections, Mr. Traldi, to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't have any particularly strong objections to it being marked, Your Honour, but I'm not sure there has been any particular foundation laid with the witness. The document has been put to him, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, sometimes the -- but if you have no real objections, then we will ask Mr. Registrar to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1460 receives number D413, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D413 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, please, let's look at 1D1461.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the Command of the 4th Corps dated 7 May 1991 -- 1992. The title is: "Events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correlation to and repercussions of the overall situation of the JNA." Under 3, it says: "With greater or lower intensity, barracks and other military installations are constantly under blockade. The personnel is being provoked and subjected to armed attacks." Would you agree with me that without co-ordination, it was not impossible [as interpreted] to attack the barracks and the personnel of the JNA in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Or do you believe that those were isolated incidents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this question, are you saying it was "not impossible" or it was "not possible"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We claim that it's not possible to have barracks attacked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Read the question on the record and correct it accordingly, if that's what you want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Without co-ordination it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult to answer the question without more information. Is a barracks attacked -- could it be attacked without co-ordination? Yes. Are you asking me specifically about the barracks in Sarajevo, for example, or -- it -- it -- I would like you to be a little more specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is discussed here is the overall situation of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see in the Krajina area in this period of April - and I know this goes into May - in the Krajina, I did not see large-scale co-ordinated attacks or co-ordinated attacks against the JNA except with the possible exception of the corridor, where the Croats took control of the corridor, I believe, it was March - I'd have to check my report - and there were some incidents in the border area around Bugojno, I think. But in the Krajina, I did not see large-scale co-ordinated attacks against the JNA. In part, the 5th Corps was working in Western Slavonia. Part of its corps was there, so there were certainly operations against that corps in that area. But internally in Bosnia, in the Krajina, I did not see large-scale co-ordinated attacks against the JNA. There were in May certainly lower-level, relatively low-level attacks. But if you asked about co-ordinated attacks against the JNA in the 5th Corps in particular or 1st Krajina Corps as it developed into, I did not see that from their reports. Now I am aware -- it's not a part of this report, but my background knowledge -- I am aware that some barracks in Sarajevo and elsewhere were surrounded, were attacked, and certainly that would have caused tensions, did rise -- give a rise to tension, and most likely you would have to have some degree of co-ordination in order to block that. But if you're underlying question to me is that did I see large-scale co-ordinated attacks against the JNA in April or May, in particular, I didn't see in the Krajina, from the documents that I have reviewed from the -- own corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's rather a long answer, but I'll ask you briefly: Derventa, that is to say, the barracks in Derventa, is a part of the 1st Krajina Corps, that is to say, the 5th Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that barracks occupied by the Croat-Muslim forces? And did they, on the axis Bosanski Brod-Derventa-Doboj occupy everything, take hold of everything, in depth towards Doboj along a stretch of 60 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness earlier made an exception to the corridor. Are we talking about the corridor at this moment or close to the corridor? My knowledge of where Derventa is -- is -- well, just at the norther -- close to the northern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would call it corridor. Corridor is some narrow stretch of land. This is one of the widest area in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you include Derventa in your exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It's that general area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What else, according to you, would be a corridor? What other things did those forces occupy?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the corridor was severed by Croat forces in that area at that time. I believe it was in March 1992. I think the area also was split between the 5th Corps and the neighbouring corps, which was the 17th Corps. So it wasn't just in the 5th Corps zone. But, as I said, Croat forces took control of that area in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number 1D1461 receives number D414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D414 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you're aware of some general things about the attack on the JNA column in Tuzla which happened in mid-May.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details of an attack on a column in Tuzla. It wasn't really in my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you hear what happened in Sarajevo at the beginning of May 1992? There was another attack also on a column.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that generally. It -- because it has been well reported, but it's not part of my -- my report. Yes, I know that this column was -- a JNA column was split.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at your paragraph 1.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English, it will be on page 15 and it will spill over onto page 16. And in e-court, it is page 16, continuing on page 17, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come across a single document in which the JNA declares a war on Bosnian Muslims, like the Muslim officials did against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen the instruction about the Bosnian Muslims declaring a war on the JNA, so I can't really comment on that. I haven't seen a JNA document with that wording, declaring war on -- on Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is what happens if you put a question and combine it with a comment and giving evidence yourself, then the witness, of course, doesn't know where to start with answering your question or to -- commenting on your observations. Could you please split them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm happy with this answer and I will [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, but for future purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever come across a document in which the Serbian attack -- side orders attacks on the JNA barracks, officers, their families, in which they order the arrests and killings of JNA soldiers? Did you ever come across a document like that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe -- I don't believe I did, if I -- if I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did, and I thank you. And by way of conclusion, would it be right to say that the JNA sided with the only side in Bosnia and Herzegovina that never attacked it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain exactly what you mean by that question, Mr. Lukic, because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how else to put this question to make it sound better and clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the JNA, for example, moved its equipment to the territory which was not under the control of the Muslim and Croat forces which is only normal. Because if they moved to the territory under the control of the Muslim and Croat sides, they would have been attacked there, wouldn't they? That's why they decided to move their equipment and troops to the territory under the Serbian control, because they were safe there. They were not attacked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's your explanation. It's apparently the answer you expect the witness to give. But could you put it in -- the -- the question was rather vague to me. I mean, if you say, You side with the party which doesn't attack you, if you would do the opposite and you say, The party with which you side you do not attack. That's -- it's -- it's all sweeping, abstract statements. Ask for specific conclusions or -- but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, in Mr. Brown's work, we do come across various explanations as to why the JNA sided with the Serbs, and I'm now offering my own explanation for that and I'm asking him whether such an explanation would be acceptable or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you then are supposed to do is to take him to the place where he draws any conclusions and then ask him whether on the basis, on the factual basis, underlying that conclusion whether you could exclude for another explanation and then you give the explanation. That's fair to do, no problem. But then put it in such a way that everyone understands exactly what you are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But a large number of pages deal with this issue. I cannot cite all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you start with two or three, then we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll move to paragraph 1.18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say even when the corps emphasised the fact that it was supporting all the ethnic groups, special emphasise was put on the danger threatening Serbs. And from the corps reports, one could gather that members of the other groups would be protected if they support the political settlement that resulted in some kind of new federal Yugoslavia. And then you cite a document of the 5th Corps, and you take as an example of the JNA siding with the Serbs in Slavonia. Did you know that in October 1990, the Croatian minister of defence, Martin Spegelj, was recorded on video camera planning a massacre of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that video, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was broadcast for a long time in all the media. Did you know then in early January 1991 the minister of the interior of Croatia, Josip Boljkovac, was recorded planning the expulsion of Serbs from Croatia, or, in his words, that there would be no more Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unaware of that, and I'm not able to comment on it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the words of President Tudjman, that the strike against the Serbs should be so forceful that the Serbs practically disappear?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that either, sir. It wasn't part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you had known about these statements, would you have accepted that the protection of the Serb people in Croatia by the JNA was justified, or would you still see it as partiality?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can easily answer that question, sir. The -- as far as I'm aware, the -- the -- the function of the JNA as a federal body was to protect the territory and to -- to protect all peoples irrespective of their ethnicity. In -- as it developed, the operations that the JNA conducted certainly in the latter part of 1992 -- 1991 in Croatia were about the protection of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Was the JNA attacked in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I don't know the details, but I'm -- yeah, I'm sure on some occasions it was. It was not an area of my study that I know well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the JNA was attacked in some places. There was a conflict there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the conflict started? Did the JNA first attack citizens of Croatia, or was it JNA personnel in barracks who were attacked first?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, I don't know the chronology well. I do know there were barracks that were surrounded and attacked. As to the chronology, the context and the build-up, it's not an area of my study in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now we'll move briefly to the organisation of non-Serb formations in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps and the mode of attack. On page 9 of your report --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, we need to move to the next page because the passage I need begins at the bottom. It says: "The inhabitants of several non-Serb villages in certain municipalities had attempted to organise themselves and in some areas had established a Crisis Staff/Territorial Defence force. Some amounts of weaponry had been procured ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you -- are you aware that the Muslim side began its military organising not later than March 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWAN McGREGOR BROWN [Resumed]
